The science of archaeology (study of antiquity) was first applied to the Sarpy Creek area in 1972 when Westmoreland Resources and the Burlington Northern Railroad contracted with the University of Montana to conduct extensive archaeological surveys in their respective areas of proposed mining and related activities. Sites of prehistoric activities such as vision-quest cairns, rock art, rock shelters, and open camp grounds were discovered.
Within Westmoreland's Tract III the university investigators initially located and confirmed eight sites. These sites include a cluster of nine vision-quest cairns on a high hill, three small lithic materials areas, three brief period habitation sites, and one habitation site used intermittently since 3,000 P.C. (as evidenced by McKean points).
During the summer of 1975, the Montana College of Mineral Science & Technology conducted initial archaeological surveys in Westmoreland's Tract II and further surveyed areas in Tract III not covered by the University of Montana's work of 1972. A total of sixty-nine new sites, thirty-five in Tract II and thirty-four in Tract III, were found.
These were categorized into the following site types: fifty-three open occupation, three observation, two quarry, two rock art, seven tepms or stone rings, one rock cairn, and one chipping station.
